title: Casper and the Bell
premise: Oscar Villalobos, a hospice nurse who has spent her life refusing to believe in anything she can't chart, hears the dying count backwards from ten — and when she reaches her mother's old house for the reading of the will, the imaginary friend she invented at age seven is sitting on the porch, unchanged by twenty years. Casper tells her that something was invited in the winter her mother died, something that wears the frost on the windows as a signature, and that it has been keeping Oscar 'safe' — invisible, unloved, untouched — ever since. To survive until sunrise, Oscar must finally believe, and must choose between the protection that has hollowed out her life and the terrible, loving truth of what her mother bargained away. She breaks the invitation at dawn, losing Casper forever but walking into the cold as a person the frost can finally see.
about_author: Dominic Yarrow is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent six years in residential hospice work before turning to fiction full-time. They write horror about the quiet violence of being kept safe, and live somewhere with very long winters.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the hospice, Mr. Abernathy counts backwards from ten for six hours before dying, smiling the whole time. Oscar documents it clinically, refuses the obvious interpretation. Emotional beat: the armor of professionalism, and the first crack in it when she catches herself whispering 'one' along with him.

chapters.title: Notice of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A lawyer's letter: her estranged mother's house in Hollow Creek is hers, on the condition she stay one night — the night of the first frost. Her coworker Marisol begs her not to go. Emotional beat: dread disguised as annoyance; Oscar packs like she's preparing for a medical emergency, not a homecoming.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She arrives at dusk. The house is exactly as her mother left it, down to the unwashed mug. On the porch swing sits Casper — her imaginary friend from age seven, a boy of about ten with frost-white eyes, unchanged. Emotional beat: vertigo. She does the sensible thing and tries to leave; the road loops back to the porch.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. He explains the terms: the house is 'held' until sunrise, something else is coming with the frost, and Oscar must not open the door, answer the phone, or look at the windows after midnight. He is gentle, patient, heartbreakingly glad to see her. Emotional beat: warmth with an undertow — Casper loves her, and that love feels like a cage she's lived in for twenty years.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Exploring the house, she finds her childhood drawings — every one features Casper, and in the later ones, something tall standing behind him. Her mother's journals are mostly burnt, but one page survives: 'It only wanted what was already mine to give.' Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: First Knock
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Frost crawls up the windows in patterns like handwriting. Something knocks — a polite, patient knock, in a rhythm her mother used to signal dinner. Casper tells her not to answer. She almost doesn't. Emotional beat: the horror of the familiar; the thing outside knows her childhood better than she does.

chapters.title: The Phone Rings
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, intercut with Marisol's. Marisol calls in a panic — she's been dreaming of Oscar's house, of a voice counting backwards. The call degrades into static, then into her mother's voice, then into Oscar's own. Casper cuts the line. Emotional beat: isolation closing in; the first time Oscar is genuinely grateful for Casper.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Safe
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Flashback: how Casper was made — a child's invention given weight by something older, tasked with one job: keep Oscar invisible, unremarkable, unloved, because love is a doorway. We see every friendship he quietly ended, every romance he smothered. Emotional beat: tender, monstrous devotion; Casper believes he has been her salvation.

chapters.title: The Neighbor
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A woman, Ruthie, appears at the edge of the yard with a lantern — a childhood neighbor, aged decades since yesterday, it seems. She shouts that Oscar's mother made a bargain in the frost winter and that Casper is not Oscar's friend, he's the payment plan. The frost takes Ruthie mid-sentence, politely, like closing a door. Emotional beat: the first hard evidence that Casper has lied.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Oscar and Casper, alternating. She demands the truth. He admits the arrangement but insists it saved her life — the thing outside wanted her whole, or wanted her at all. 'You were dying of loneliness and I kept you alive.' Emotional beat: rage and gratitude in the same breath; Oscar realizes she cannot tell protector from jailer.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Midnight. The window frost resolves into words: a full accounting of the bargain — her mother traded Oscar's visibility for her survival, and the debt compounds yearly. Tonight is the final collection. Emotional beat: cold clarity; the horror is bureaucratic, patient, and signed in her mother's hand.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, the buried memory. The winter her mother was dying, she invited something in to spare Oscar the loss — and it came, and it stayed, and Casper was its collateral, its leash, its apology. Casper was never imaginary; he was the down payment. Emotional beat: Casper's own grief; he was made to be loved and used in the same gesture.

chapters.title: The Second Knock
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The knocking becomes her own voice, then her mother's, then silence — worse than all of it. The house begins exhaling cold. Casper weakens; the frost is reclaiming him. Emotional beat: the protector failing, and Oscar discovering she does not want him to go, which frightens her more than the thing outside.

chapters.title: Marisol at the Door
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Near 3 a.m., Marisol's car is in the driveway — but Marisol is still on the phone at home, sobbing, so the Marisol at the door is a lure. It speaks in Oscar's mother's voice, offering forgiveness if Oscar just opens up. Emotional beat: the cruelest test yet; love weaponized; Oscar presses her hand to the door and weeps without opening it.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the cellar she finds the physical bargain: a page of ice that never melts, listing every year of her 'safety' as a withdrawal. The balance is due at sunrise. There is a clause — her mother left her one: the debt can be discharged by the one who holds it, if she chooses visibility over protection. Emotional beat: hope with a price tag; Oscar understands what 'choosing' means.

chapters.title: Casper's Confession
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. He tells her everything, finally, and offers the way out: if she renounces him — truly, from love and not fear — the invitation breaks and the thing outside loses its claim. But he will unmake with it. He asks her not to. Emotional beat: the love-against-duty theme made flesh; both of them know what she has to do and neither can say it.

chapters.title: The Thing in the Frost
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. 5 a.m. The windows go black with frost and she finally sees it: vast, patient, shaped like the negative space of everyone who ever stopped seeing her. It shows her a vision of the life Casper saved her from — and the life she could have had. Emotional beat: the temptation of the cage, rendered beautiful; the lowest, coldest point.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Oscar and Casper. She drafts her refusal like a nurse writing a chart — precise, unsentimental, true. She tells Casper she doesn't renounce him out of fear but releases him out of love, and that she will remember him, which the thing never counted on. Emotional beat: quiet, trembling resolve; the decision made in the last dark hour.

chapters.title: The Unmaking
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. As she speaks the release, Casper comes apart into warm light and frost-mist, and for one moment he is every age she imagined him at, all at once, saying her name — her real name, the one no one uses. The thing outside shrieks like a kettle and the ice page shatters. Emotional beat: grief and liberation indistinguishable; the sacrifice that was also a gift.

chapters.title: Dawn
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She opens the front door herself, deliberately, into ordinary cold. The road out of Hollow Creek is just a road. Marisol arrives, real, furious, relieved. Emotional beat: raw, hungover survival; the strange lightness of a person the world can see again.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, weeks later. Back at the hospice, a dying patient begins counting backwards and Oscar holds her hand and counts with her, unafraid. She has lost the protection that cost her a life, and gained the weight of being visible — every risk of it. Emotional beat: mourning as evidence of love; the theme answered.

chapters.title: Frost on the Inside of the Glass
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. First frost of the next winter. On her apartment window, inside the glass, a small handprint of frost appears, and beside it, faintly, a child's drawing of two figures holding hands. Oscar doesn't open the door. She smiles, and says 'one,' and lets the pattern finish. Emotional beat: bittersweet coda — some loves outlast their unmaking, and the bell, when it rings, rings both ways.
